stem: Two commodities have the following prices and base-period quantities. Commodity A: base price Rs 10, current price Rs 14, base quantity 3 units. Commodity B: base price Rs 5, current price Rs 6, base quantity 10 units. Compute the Laspeyres price index for the current period.

per_option_rationale.rationale: Computing the simple (unweighted) mean of price relatives: ((14/10 + 6/5) / 2) x 100 = (1.4 + 1.2) / 2 x 100 = 130.0. This ignores the quantity weights that define Laspeyres.
Using the simple aggregate price ratio (sum of current prices / sum of base prices): (14+6)/(10+5) x 100 = 20/15 x 100 = 133.3. This weights prices equally by inclusion rather than by quantities.
Inverting the ratio - computing sum(p0 x q0) / sum(p1 x q0) x 100 = 80/102 x 100 = 78.4. This gives the base period relative to the current period, not the other way around.

explanation: Laspeyres price index uses base-period quantities as fixed weights: P_L = [sum(p1 x q0) / sum(p0 x q0)] x 100. Numerator: 14x3 + 6x10 = 42 + 60 = 102. Denominator: 10x3 + 5x10 = 30 + 50 = 80. Index = 102/80 x 100 = 127.5. Commodity B dominates (q0=10) so the lower price rise of B (20%) pulls the index below A's price rise (40%).

explanation_sections.punchline: Laspeyres weights each price change by the base-period quantity; larger-volume commodities have a stronger pull on the index.
explanation_sections.approach: Name the formula: Laspeyres = sum(p1*q0) / sum(p0*q0) x 100. Map: multiply each commodity's current price by its base quantity (numerator) and base price by base quantity (denominator). Sum and divide.
explanation_sections.lesson: Laspeyres always uses base-period quantities (q0). Paasche uses current-period quantities (q1). Mixing them up is the most common error.
explanation_sections.timing: About 75 seconds. Trap: option 2 (130) is the mean price relative and a very common wrong path. Verify: both methods give the same answer only when all quantities are equal.
